# `testing/no-conditional-expect`

**No `expect` inside a condition**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pack** | `@codelaw/rules-testing` (npm) |
| **Languages** | JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX |
| **Turned on by** | `codelaw:testing/jest` at `error` · `codelaw:testing/vitest` at `error` |
| **Severity when named without one** | `error` |
| **Options** | none — severity only |
| **Fix** | `manual` — no automatic fix; the steps are under *How to fix* (the test has to be split or its setup fixed so the assertion always runs; no edit can tell which) |
| **Stability** | `preview` — runs only with `preview = true` |
| **Since** | 0.5.0 |
| **Files** | only `**/*.test.*`, `**/*.spec.*`, `**/__tests__/**`, `**/test/**`, `**/tests/**`, `**/e2e/**` |
| **Ported from** | `eslint-plugin-jest/no-conditional-expect`, `@vitest/eslint-plugin/no-conditional-expect` |

## What it checks

A test does not call `expect` inside an `if`, a `switch`, a `catch`, a `? :` or a `&&`/`||`, where it may silently not run.

**Why:** A conditional assertion passes when the condition is false, so the test can pass while checking nothing.

## Configuration

Everything below goes in `codelaw.toml` at the repo root. The same keys work as `[tool.codelaw]` in `pyproject.toml` or `"codelaw"` in `package.json` ([SR-CONFIG](../../../records/0110_config.md)).

### Turn it on

**Install the pack** (`codelaw init` does it for the languages it finds):

```bash
npm install --save-dev @codelaw/rules-testing
```

**Then extend a preset that turns it on** — `codelaw:testing/jest` sets it to `error`:

```toml
preview = true                        # pack rules are preview today
extends = ["codelaw:testing/jest"]
```

- **A rule exists only once its pack is loaded** through `extends`; naming it in `[rules]` without that is an unknown rule id (exit 2).
- **Without `preview = true`** the rule is skipped and codelaw warns that it is preview.

### Severity

```toml
[rules]
"testing/no-conditional-expect" = "warn"    # error | warn | info | off
```

- **`error`** fails the run (exit 1) · **`warn`** fails only with `--max-warnings N` · **`info`** never fails · **`off`** turns it off.
- **Naming it with a severity turns it on** even when no preset does.

### For a group of files

A `[scope.<name>]` gives some files their own setting, applied after `[rules]` — the `tests` scope `codelaw:js/recommended` ships (`**/*.test.*`, `**/*.spec.*`); naming it extends it, so its files stay:

```toml
[scope.tests]
rules = { "testing/no-conditional-expect" = "off" }
```

A scope's `remap` changes whole severities in its files, after everything else: `remap = { error = "warn" }` never fails the run there.

### Warn locally, fail in CI

The `ci` profile runs when `CI` is set; `local` otherwise; `--profile <name>` or `CODELAW_PROFILE` picks one.

```toml
[profile.local.rules]
"testing/no-conditional-expect" = "warn"

[profile.ci.rules]
"testing/no-conditional-expect" = "error"
```

### In `pyproject.toml` or `package.json`

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[tool.codelaw.rules]
"testing/no-conditional-expect" = { severity = "warn" }
```

```json
{
  "codelaw": {
    "rules": {
      "testing/no-conditional-expect": {"severity": "warn"}
    }
  }
}
```

### Silence one finding

An inline `codelaw-ignore` always needs a reason; `expires=`, `warn_days=` and `by=` date it ([SR-LINTER](../../../records/0106_linter.md) decision 6).

- **JavaScript:** `// codelaw-ignore testing/no-conditional-expect: <reason>`
- **Dated:** `// codelaw-ignore testing/no-conditional-expect expires=2026-12-31 by=you@example.com: <reason>`

### Keep today's findings, fail on new ones

```bash
codelaw baseline add --rule testing/no-conditional-expect --expires 2026-12-31 --reason "<why>"
```

See [SR-BASELINE](../../../records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md).

### See what applies

```bash
codelaw explain testing/no-conditional-expect       # what it wants, why, how to fix
codelaw check --rule testing/no-conditional-expect  # only this rule
codelaw config --print --for <file>                 # the resolved setting, and where it came from
```

## How to fix

1. Split the test so each case sets up the state it asserts on, and assert unconditionally.
2. For an expected error, use `expect(() => …).toThrow()` or `await expect(p).rejects…` instead of `try`/`catch`.

## Examples

### JavaScript

#### Don't

```js
test("parses", () => {
  if (input) {
    expect(parse(input)).toBe(1);
  }
});
```

#### Do

```js
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
});
```

### JSX

#### Don't

```jsx
test("parses", () => {
  if (input) {
    expect(parse(input)).toBe(1);
  }
});
```

#### Do

```jsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
});
```

### TypeScript

#### Don't

```ts
test("parses", () => {
  if (input) {
    expect(parse(input)).toBe(1);
  }
});
```

#### Do

```ts
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
});
```

### TSX

#### Don't

```tsx
test("parses", () => {
  if (input) {
    expect(parse(input)).toBe(1);
  }
});
```

#### Do

```tsx
test("parses", () => {
  expect(parse("1")).toBe(1);
});
```
